o: We repeatedly build the result in waves: each wave first appends characters in strictly increasing order (smallest available, then next larger, etc.), then appends remaining characters in strictly decreasing order, until the string is empty. For `"aaaabbbbcccc"`, wave 1 takes one of each letter a→b→c giving "abc", then c→b→a giving "abccba"; with s = "aabbcc" left, wave 2 produces "abc" then "cba", yielding "abccbaabccba". For `"rat"`, the increasing pass gives "ar" (a then r), and the decreasing pass adds "t", so the answer is "art". Since n ≤ 500 and only 26 lowercase letters exist, even a naive simulation that rescans counts every step is fast; the key realization is that we only need character counts, not the actual string.
k: The algorithm only depends on character frequencies — simulate on a 26-size count array instead of mutating strings.
Each 'wave' is: scan letters ascending picking any with count > 0, then scan descending doing the same; repeat until all counts are zero.
With at most 26 distinct letters per pass, total work is O(n · 26) regardless of how many waves occur.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute-force simulation on the string
a.i: Directly follow the algorithm's wording: keep the string as a list, and for each step linearly search for the smallest/largest remaining character satisfying the strict inequality against the last appended character. This mirrors the problem statement exactly and is easy to reason about, though it does redundant scanning.
s: Convert s to a list of characters used as a multiset.
While the list is non-empty: append the minimum remaining character, then repeatedly find and remove the smallest remaining character strictly greater than the last appended one.
Then append the maximum remaining character, and repeatedly remove the largest remaining character strictly smaller than the last appended one.
Repeat until the list is empty and return the joined result.
a.t: O(n²) — each removal scans the remaining list of up to n characters, and there are n removals.
a.sp: O(n) — for the working list and result builder.

a.i: Since only 26 letters exist, keep a count array. Each wave is two fixed 26-element scans: an ascending scan appending every letter whose count is still positive (this automatically yields the increasing sequence), then a descending scan doing the same. Repeat until n characters have been appended. This is dramatically simpler and faster than searching/removing from a list.
s: Build cnt[26] from s and initialize an empty result.
While the result length is less than n:
Scan i from 0 to 25; whenever cnt[i] > 0, decrement it and append the letter (increasing pass).
Scan i from 25 down to 0; whenever cnt[i] > 0, decrement it and append the letter (decreasing pass).
a.t: O(n) — each character is appended exactly once, plus O(26) overhead per wave; total is O(n + 26·waves) ⊆ O(n·26) but effectively linear since waves ≤ n.
a.sp: O(1) extra — fixed 26-entry count array (excluding the output).

w: In an interview, state the brute force briefly to show you understand the mechanics, then pivot to the counting approach — it's the expected solution given the Hash Table/Counting tags. Key pitfalls: forgetting that duplicates are consumed one occurrence per pass (so "aaabbb" → "abab"), breaking out of the loop correctly when the decreasing pass empties the string mid-wave, and off-by-one errors when checking loop termination. Edge cases: single-character strings, all-identical characters (e.g., "aaaa" → "aaaa"), and already-sorted input. Likely follow-ups: generalize to arbitrary alphabets (use a sorted map or bucket structure), or handle uppercase/mixed characters by widening the count array.
